title: Metta Sutta 2
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the commentary's story of where the Metta Sutta comes from: 500 monks who go north to the Himalayan foothills for the rains retreat and are driven out by tree spirits with frightening sights, sounds, and smells. The Buddha sends them back chanting the sutta, and the spirits welcome them. Partners then discuss the sutta's fifteen virtues, including whether "unburdened with duties" means having none or not carrying them as a burden. Nomon returns to the text with the Pali words for well-being, safety, and happiness in the third verse. The list of beings in verse four ends with the five realms, read both literally and as states of mind.

I want to start today's class, as promised, with the story of where the Metta Sutta came from, according to the commentaries.
This is not in the Nikkaya, it's not in the Pali canon.
But I'm learning more and more that, in addition to the canon itself, there's a quite important and pretty ancient set of commentaries.
A traditional, early Buddhist monk would always have both, side by side.
These commentaries were written down starting more or less in the birth of Christ time.
The ones that survived were probably written mostly in southern India, in Sri Lanka.
They mostly were written, I guess, in Sinhalese, which is the language of Sri Lanka.
Then later they were organized and translated, forward or back, depending on how you think about it, into Pali, to give them a little more ecclesiastical oomph and staying power.
The southern monks of Sri Lanka and South India were invested in Pali as the lingua franca of Buddhism, so this was part of that effort, apparently.
And with a little domineering style, as all human beings like to do, right?
Anyway, this story is from the commentary.
Whether it's true or not, who knows, but who knows that about anything.
So the story is, one time the Buddha was teaching in the town of Savasthi.
He had this kind of circuit he would go.
It was a little bit before the rains retreat, the annual practice period, which is the monsoon season.
During the monsoon season, the monks and nuns would try to find one place and not travel as much.
I always thought it was because the roads are bad.
But it turns out it's because you do damage the crops if you walk in any fields, so out of respect and protectiveness of the crops.
And Fran knows another detail.
**Participant:** Also because the animals would come up in the mud and they would squish and kill you.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, okay.
So three likely reasons: bad roads, worms, and farms.
Anyway, it became the tradition.
It probably had some basis in practicality, but it was actually a religious observance.
So it's almost that time.
The monks have got to figure out where they're going to spend the rains, because then you're not supposed to move.
A bunch of monks were with the Buddha getting instructions before this long retreat.

I'm going to read you the translation of the description of the instructions, because one thing that's neat about the early Buddha stories is they give you a little window into how the Buddha operated.
So it says,
*The Buddha expounded meditation subjects suitable for the 84,000 shades of temperament.*
We're all different.
There are 84,000 versions of people, and he has a different subject for each one.
*And there he had expounded meditation subjects for these 84,000 shades of temperament in the following way.
And for those of lustful temperament, he showed loathsomeness as a meditation subject of the 11 kinds, as with consciousness and without consciousness.*
So, different teachings for people who are lustful.
*For those of hating temperament, he taught the fourfold mindfulness subject beginning with loving kindness.
For those of deluded temperament, he taught the meditation subject consisting of mindfulness of death.
For those of a speculative thinking temperament,*
that's us, right, speculative thinking temperament,
*he taught the mindfulness of breathing, the earth, universal, etc.
And for those of a faithful temperament, the subjects consisted of the recollection of the enlightened ones, etc.*
I think "etc." stands for a big long list of teachings that we don't know.
*And for those of intelligent or discerning temperament, he taught the definition of the four elements.*
So, different stuff for different folks.
And then amongst this enormous group of monks, huge numbers of monks, it says there's a group of 500 monks.
I guess 500 is a sort of canonical code for a lot of them.
It doesn't mean exactly 500.
These 500 monks were quite impressed with his teachings and wanted to go a little further away than all the other ones, to a really quiet spot to practice.
So they hiked their way, mindfully walked their way, for several days to the foothills of the Himalaya.
They went north.
They found a really beautiful spot.
The story says they found a spot where
*the surface,*
I'm not sure the surface is a what, a lake maybe,
*the surface glittered like blue quartz crystal.
It was embellished with a cool, dense, shady, green forest grove and a stretch of ground strewn with sand resembling a net or a silver sheet.
And it was furnished with a clean spring of grateful, cool water.*
That's grateful, cool water: water that is grateful to be drunk.
So they found a really good spot and they did a night of meditation.
They were quite happy and overjoyed with their beautiful spot for meditation.
They went into the town the next morning, as they would, like we talked about last week, for their daily food with their bowls.
The villagers were really happy with them too.
They were peaceful, wonderful monks, and the villagers were so happy to have monks there.
This is on the little outskirts, which usually don't have fully ordained people there, I guess.
They were so happy that they begged the monks to definitely stay there for the rains retreat, and gave them really nice food.
And it says they made them huts, 500 huts.
In one day they made 500 huts.
So they had a really good lumber store there too, I guess.
Which included, it says,
*such necessities as beds, chairs, pots and so on.*
So this little village had everything needed for the 500 monks.
And there's some stuff about another village that was happy with them.
So everyone around there was really happy with them.
It started out great.
They felt so welcome.
They did a very rigorous schedule of meditation in the afternoon and throughout the night, and mostly alone in their little huts.
But then they'd come together every morning to gather, check in and go into the town for begging.
For the first few days, everyone looked great, radiant, peaceful.
The teachings were really in action.
Things were good.
It says in there that they were like royalty.
They were so beautiful in their practice.
But then after a few nights, they started having some trouble.
In the middle of the night, they started having disturbing visions during their meditation and hearing creepy sounds.
And they felt, let's see, I'll read you some of this.
*They were dreadful, it appeared to be like they were dreadful, fantastical things right in front of them making terrible sounds.
And there were forms and noises.*
And then the bhikkhus, the monks, became pale and jaundiced and could no longer unify their cognizance.
They couldn't focus.
They couldn't concentrate.
So the nights get really long when these weird things are happening.
And when they'd gather in the morning, they were all too embarrassed to say what was going on.
But after a while you can tell everyone else seems to be a wreck too.
It's not just you.
They're like us, I think.
They all thought, "Oh, it's just me.
I'm not doing this right.
The others are quite peaceful."
And then it says, finally, the leader asked them what's going on.
*The senior elder of the committee asked the other monks, "Friends, when you first entered into this wood, the color of your skin was quite pure and bright, and your faculties were clear.
But now you are lean and pale and jaundiced.
What does not suit you here?"*
What's going on?
And one of the monks finally admitted what was going on.
He said, "Venerable Sir, at night I saw and heard such and such a dreadful object.
I smelt," oh yeah, terrible smells too, really stinky smells, "I smelt such and such a terrible smell, and my mind could not be concentrated and I could not practice."
Then one by one they all copped to having this terrible experience all night.
And so they decided, what do you do when you're down?
They had to go talk to the Buddha.
So they told the villagers they had to go talk to the Buddha, and they went on.
It doesn't say how long they walked, but I'm always struck by these stories of early Buddhism in all the Asian countries: the monks spend quite a bit of time walking.
And I think that's a core part of their practice.
It doesn't get written about so much, I think, because it was so ordinary.
That's how everyone got around.
But I think we might benefit from walking when it goes to the southwest.
You should walk there.
You should probably roll a lot here.
Yeah, you have to get another hip by the time you get there.

So anyway, they went to the Buddha, and the Buddha, with his incredible divine powers, he has all these powers, he could tell what was going on: that there were earth spirits in that neck of the woods.
Sometimes they're called earth spirits or devas, sometimes they're called tree devas, who were quite happy in their woods and felt a little invaded by the monks.
And I guess it was like when somebody comes to stay with you.
It was a pretty nice person.
You're glad to have them stay for a night.
And then the next day you notice that they are quite comfortable in your refrigerator.
And then you overhear them on your phone, ordering something, and having it mailed to your house, and like that.
I think the idea of the story is that the tree spirits are not particularly malevolent spirits, but they were not pleased with this invasion of 500 monks.
And they worked together to scare the monks away, to have some peace.
And so the Buddha could tell this, and the Buddha said that what they should do is, oh, the Buddha was at first a little alarmed, excuse me, I'm telling this to everyone.
The Buddha was first a little alarmed that they showed up, because the rains had already started.
*Bhikkhu, it is a training rule that has been made known by me that no one should go wandering during the rains.
Why are you wandering?*
What are you doing back here?
And so they explained all that, and you could tell it was the tree devas.
And then he told them, well, what you should do is you need a powerful teaching to help you, and it will also help these spirits.
And so he composed on the spot and taught them the Metta Sutta.
So that's where the Metta Sutta comes from, according to the story.
And he told them that they should memorize and recite the Metta Sutta, which I think is an important point for us, because we tend to see texts as vehicles for content, you know what I mean?
That the words are a nice container, and we always want to know what's inside so we can consume it, and then we don't really care about the container.
But the suttas are understood in a little bit different way, in that the sutra or the sutta itself is an object of veneration and study and support.

So the sutta is often mentioned, and the Mahayana sutra is even more so, that just memorizing one line from the sutra is more powerful than any practice you could do, just reciting one line or having faith in one line in the sutra.
And so that's a big part of the Buddhist tradition, which we can work with and think about: it's not about the content.
It's about the actual sutra itself.
And so he told them to memorize and recite and chant this sutra.
And they said, "Oh, okay, but isn't there somewhere else we can practice?
It's kind of creepy up there.
We don't really want to go back there.
Well, we'll do this practice, but we really don't want to go back there."
What would be a better place to practice?
The Buddha cast his vision out in each direction, and it goes into great detail.
He looked first to the northeast, and then to the east.
He looked all over the world for a good place, and he looked everywhere that he could, and he could see everywhere.
He said, "Well, the only good place for you to practice is that exact spot.
That's the only place that you can practice this."
And they said, "Okay."
They hiked back, chanting the metta sutra as they went.
As they approached the spot back in the woods, they were reciting the sutra, and the spirits could hear that, and they were overjoyed.
The whole situation was fixed up.
There are various versions of the story where the tree deities fly down and help them and hold their stuff and get them all set up and really welcome them back.
So that's where the metta sutra came from, according to the commentary.
That's a nice story.
Last time, we didn't really have so much time for discussion, and you didn't really get to speak with each other, which I value as more me sending out material, which I'm glad you enjoyed.
But I thought we'd pause on that mode and spend some time in discussion of these 15 virtues that are listed in the beginning of the sutra for those who would like to practice in this way.
Let's see how many people we have here.
Six of you, that's good.
I think we'll break up for a few minutes with a partner, and I'm going to give you another handout that has these virtues listed on it.
Let's bring up together the question of these virtues.
Is this a good list?
Are these the ones you would have put on the list if something seemed missing or strange or inapplicable?
There were the two or three items that we discussed last time that seemed to be targeted directly at monks and nuns living this very simple lifestyle.

How can we work with these qualities, especially the ones about not having too many responsibilities, not being too busy, and also the one that we talked about that was the most difficult to translate, about support from family or support for family?
Are those ones that we need to turn in some way, or can we work with them directly?
Let's just contemplate and speak with our partner about whether any of these seem harder or easier to work with.

What's really hard for me about being gentle and receptive is such and so.
Let's just spend a few minutes on that and see how we relate to all this before we go on with the actual practice of metta as it's described in the next section.
Let me give you five copies of this, so we might need to share.
Let me pass this out.
Thanks.
As we're passing this out, let me remind you a little about the format of this.
We'll go with our partner off to different corners of the room where we don't hear the others as much.
We'll sit close together so we can hear each other.
Then I'll ring a bell and we'll just meditate for a moment.
Not to figure out what we're going to say or figure anything out, but just to settle.
Then we'll take turns speaking and listening.
The thing about this is that when your partner is speaking, you really just practice listening, just letting the words come in without reaction or response, just bearing witness.
It's more like bearing witness than having a conversation.
And not to do the social reassurances that we usually do: "Uh-huh, yeah, that reminds me of something."
Just listen, just let the person speak.

If the person who's speaking runs out of things to say in the five minutes or so, which would be nice, because usually we don't have more than two minutes, because I'm always jamming this in at the end, so see, I'm doing it in the middle.
Anyway, if you can't think of anything else to say, then just sit quietly and see if anything else comes up.
Sometimes you say what's obvious to yourself, or what you think the other person wants to hear on some level, and then you sit quietly for a while and you realize something else that you want to say.
So we'll give our partner the space to do that.
We won't say, "Oh, well, if you're done, I'll start early."
We'll do the whole five minutes.
Let's also agree that whatever we say in these conversations can stay here in this room, can be private, and we won't bring it up later.

We'll just let it be here so that we all still feel free to say whatever is true for us right now, you know what I mean?
Which might not be true for us after we leave.
These things change.
So let's let it be a quiet bearing witness, and not anything we really keep track of.
Just something we speak from this moment.
Okay, should we do that?
Maybe we break up pretty obviously in pairs here.
Why don't you head off to the corner with your partner, and if you don't know each other's names, be sure and introduce yourself.

Does it make sense to share?
Did you think of anything interesting?
You don't have to share anything too private, but yeah.

Unburdened with duties.

That's really good for this.
In the middle of the third stanza it breaks to the second section, which is: how do you actually do this?
What is the practice of metta, and how do you approach it?
The other thing I'm learning, and it's interesting that Fran brought up the English translation that's sung, is that I think it's a central practice that you sing these things.

It'll go...

These words are interesting to look at in detail because this is the hinge of the whole sutra.
So with my newfound Pali knowledge, which is all cribbed from other scholars, I'm going to sound very smart now.
This phrase starts and ends with two different versions of the same word.
Did you notice that?
That's suki, suki no, suki tata.
These are versions of the word suka.
We've heard of the word duka, which is suffering in different ways.
This is the opposite.
This is happiness.
So it starts and ends with happiness.
The question is why it says happiness twice.

Apparently this isn't supported by the Pali construction directly, but the commentaries, and the commentaries are how people learn about these early Buddhist works, say that the first happiness, the suki no, refers to physical well-being: good health, not being ill.
The one at the end refers to what we think of as happiness, positive mental conditions.
That isn't so much gleeful joy, like jumping up and down because we got something, but a general sense of solid well-being and rootedness and happiness.
So that's the beginning and the end.
We have three types of points they're making.
The first is physical well-being.
The third is mental happiness, we could say.
And then there's one in the middle, this word kemi no, which basically means safe, safe and secure.
The kem part means a fence, like a fence around a field keeping the livestock safe.
It's from the agrarian culture, this material.
So we're fenced off, safe, protected from danger by these teachings.
The other thing that's interesting in there is that there are two different imperative verbs, two sort of synonyms.
Hontu, so suki no, va kemi no, hontu.
Hontu means may this be, may they be.
Then sabe, the next word, is all.
Satta is beings, so may this be for all beings.
And then bhavantu, the next word, is just another form of the last imperative verb.
May they really be.
So literally it's physical well-being and safety: may all beings have this, may all beings really have this, may they be happy.
So that's what it's wishing for.
I'm actually glad to learn that, because we'll talk later about different meditation practices around metta, and they often involve working with the phrase.
What I realize is that there are different translations of this phrase, and I wondered, well, what is the right phrase?
It all comes from this, so it should always have those three elements.
It turns out they're physical well-being, or health, healthiness, safety, and happiness.
The safety can be understood in a sort of literal way, like nobody's going to attack you or harm you, or no wild animals are going to eat you or something.
But we can understand safety in a metaphorical and a psychological way too, of course.
How can we really have happiness if we don't feel safe and secure?
So that establishes the next section.
This is basically saying, okay, now this is what this is really about, this is what we want.
How should you go about generating this wish for loving-kindness?
We actually don't have the word metta so far at all, as I mentioned.
That comes a little bit later.
So next we're going to have lists of beings.

I think what's interesting about these lists of beings, and Buddhist sutras are really characterized by many different lists and divisions, is that it was partly the philosophical milieu of medieval India.
They thought about things that way: okay, I mean all beings, but what do I mean when I say all?
What does that actually mean?
Well, it means this kind and that kind, and you might think I'm excluding this kind, but I'm not.
There's also this kind, and don't forget about that kind, in these long lists.
So that's one way, I think, they thought about things.
But the other shade of meaning here is that this is not just a list to make a point.
We might see it as making emphasis, and sort of cute: oh, we got it the first time, we know what all means.
We think it's kind of sweet.
But actually, when they make these long lists, they're meditation instructions.
They're saying, no, literally, you should first try to hold your mind on the feeling of loving-kindness for all beings.
But that might be a little hard to do.
So then, hold your mind on a feeling of loving-kindness towards all weak beings.
Really direct that loving-kindness towards weak beings, and this kind of beings, and then that kind of beings, and so on, step by step, very step by step.
These lists are funny for us because they're not the way we would chop it up.
We would chop it up in different ways, but we can understand it that way: realize the way that you categorize things and use that categorization as a spiritual tool.

Recognize the duality of mind and say, okay, well, since I think there are nice people and mean people, my metta meditation will be more effective if I deliberately direct it to those people who I think are mean people.
Really bring that up and acknowledge, I have that feeling.
It's an illusion, but I think that way.
And bring my meditation towards people I think are nice people, and so on.
So let me play the next verse, and I'll tell you what some of these words mean and we'll call it a day.
We got into the second section.

Remember the three categories of Buddhist teaching; they understand this sutra to address sila, or virtue, samadhi, or meditation, so this is now meditation instructions, and paññā or prajñā, or wisdom, how to apply all this wisely.
So let's listen to the next one, just starting the list.
These beings are in all different categories.
And yes, yes, it's fine.
[unclear: "I go and die and keep that style of wine Oh, I want and now I stay and die and die"]

Neat though.

The first line literally means all, again, all, whatever being.
This *pana* means all living and breathing beings.
The first line is just, again, all beings, we really mean it.
And then the list starts with the second line, *tasa va thavara va anavasesa*.
That gets translated as weak or strong, but it's interesting, actually.
I'm getting into the textual analysis.
I hope this isn't boring to you.
Okay.
All right.
So *tasa* and *thavara* mean, respectively, moving and stable, or not moving.

They run it on two axes, actually.
The first list of big, small, and medium is long ones, short ones, and medium ones.

And then the second list apparently means density.
So thick ones, dense ones, medium-density ones, and ephemeral, airy ones.

Anyway, I think it's interesting too because that wouldn't be our first cut on how to organize beings.

But the other thing to think about is that it doesn't just mean, and they're going to get into this in the next verse, which we'll do next week, they don't just mean beings that we can see and touch, either.
